name: Gareth Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Gareth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential, so give me both the public line and the private one. Can you take me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a team lead at Brightside Market, a supermarket that does a huge amount of online orders. In the morning I run the picking team, six people with handheld scanners filling crates for home delivery. In the afternoon I cover the tills and help whoever's behind. I love the pace, and I'm always trying to shave a minute off how we pick.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's tough?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy fixing a system, like moving the frozen section order and cutting our pick time by 12 percent. The tough part is substitutions. When an item's out, the customer gets angry at me, and the pay is low for the pressure. Hannah (my partner, a trainee teacher) says I talk about crates in my sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's a solid helper but nothing magic. I use it daily to write shift notes, build little spreadsheets and plan pick routes. I'd tell friends it saves me time and that people who ignore it are leaving free help on the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fine about AI, but my money is thin. I have under a month saved, rent is high, and Hannah's trainee income is small. If a car repair hits, I'm on the credit card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, use the tools better and push for a small pay bump based on the numbers I've improved. I'd put 80 a month into a savings pot and 30 into a cheap index fund, just to start the habit. And I'd carry on tinkering with a little side project: a script that helps the picking team plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite good, honestly. I'm a tinkerer and the plateau is a nice stable place to tinker. I'd still wish the cash wasn't so tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. What does it do for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month the van for Hannah's placement needed new tyres, 260 I didn't have. It went on the card, and we both laughed and then went quiet. A calm world doesn't change that bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What bills worry you even in a flat world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The industry. Supermarkets run on tiny margins and squeeze the staff, even when staff make them more efficient. If I save the shop money, I want a share of it, and I'd say so politely.

If I save the shop money, I want a **share**.
think: I'm fine about AI, but **money** is thin: under a month saved and high rent.
A surprise bill like **tyres** goes straight onto the card.
do: Use AI daily for **shift notes** and pick routes.
Put **80 a month** into savings and 30 into an index fund.
Ask for a small **pay bump** based on pick-time numbers.
feel: Quite **good**, since it's a stable place to tinker, though I wish the cash wasn't so tight.
S0.quote: Last month the van for Hannah's placement needed new tyres, 260 I didn't have. It went on the card, and we both laughed and then went quiet.
fieldNote: Technology is a **hobby** for him, so a plateau is comfortable.
His unease is entirely **financial**: rent, tyres and a trainee partner's pay.
Frames savings as **share** of value he creates, a centrist negotiating stance.

steps.text: Use AI daily for shift notes and pick-route planning
Put 80 a month into a savings pot
Start a cheap index fund with 30 a month
Build a small planning script to sell to other pick teams

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say planning and ordering go to AI, and the picking itself gets assisted by better scanners. Customers will still want a person at the door, but fewer people will do more. I'd tell friends that the shops that do it well will get stronger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us it's a mixed bag. My team lead job is half people and half logistics, and the logistics half is exactly what AI does. Soon the planning could be done by the head office system, and I'd be a person who walks around and fixes things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean in. I'd learn the new routing software inside out and offer to pilot every tool they bring in. I'd also take an online certificate in logistics or automation for about 30 a month. And I'd keep the side script going, because it's the one thing that shows I can build and not just use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and slightly nervous, which is how I like to feel at work. It's a lot to learn, and learning is the fun bit. The nervous part is still the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which jobs in your shop are the first to be handed to software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We had a pilot last spring with a system that proposes the pick order. I found it was routing people past the frozen aisle three times, flagged it, and they changed it. My manager said I was worth two of the contractors who set it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How could you make yourself harder to replace?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Be the person who understands both the floor and the system. A tool doesn't know the lift is broken or that the dairy section's cold store has a fault. A person who knows both is harder to replace, and may even get a raise.

say: Planning and ordering go to AI, and shops that do it well will get **stronger**.
think: The logistics half of my team lead job is exactly what **AI** does.
I'd end up the person who **walks around** and fixes things.
do: Learn the routing software and **pilot** every new tool.
Take an online **logistics** certificate for about 30 a month.
feel: **Excited** and slightly nervous, because the learning is the fun bit.
S1.quote: A tool doesn't know the lift is broken or that the dairy section's cold store has a fault.
fieldNote: He expects **thinking** work to go first and moves toward the floor-plus-system gap.
His **pilot** feedback gave him evidence of value, not just hope.
Mood stays uneasy because he's still on a **thin cushion**.

steps.text: Learn the new routing software and pilot every tool the shop brings in
Take an online logistics certificate for about 30 a month
Keep building the pick-planning script on evenings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say don't pretend it's a normal year. I'd gather the team and share what I know, because most of them haven't tried the tools. To friends I'd say learn it, because the people who know AI will have a head start. I'd also say governments need to move now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be anxious, not terrified. The thinking AI takes planning and logistics, which is where I was heading, and then robots reach picking and tills by 2031. I'd be 31 with no savings and a job type that's mostly gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the robot side of it. I'd aim to be a technician who installs and maintains automated picking systems, because every store would need them. I'd start an evening course and approach the supplier who installs our scanners to ask how they hire. I'd also push the side project and try to sell it to two other shops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a buzz. It's a scary situation, but I'd be one of those people running toward it. I'd hate it if Hannah and I had to move, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does 2028 change the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years is long enough to qualify. A maintenance tech has a hands-on role that sits right beside the robots, which would be late to be replaced. The risk is that a robot that fixes robots shows up in 2033.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the three years before the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the government to subsidise short courses with a living grant. Not everyone has my kind of curiosity, and a lot of my team will freeze. If I could, I'd start a small group to teach them what I learn.

say: Don't pretend it's a **normal year**: I'd share what I know with my team.
People who know **AI** will have a head start, but governments must move now.
think: Thinking AI takes planning and logistics, then **robots** reach picking and tills by 2031.
I'd be 31 with no savings and a job type that's mostly **gone**.

Try to **sell** my planning script to two other shops.
feel: **Anxious** with a buzz, running toward the change.
S2.quote: The risk is that a robot that fixes robots shows up in 2033.
fieldNote: He turns the **robot gap** into a career: maintenance beside the machines.
Worries about **coworkers** who will freeze and wants to teach them.

steps.text: Start an evening course in automated picking system maintenance

Try to sell the planning script to two other shops
Run lunch sessions to teach the picking team the tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is enough to retool the team. I'd run short sessions on the tools and ask head office to pay for courses. To friends, I'd say don't wait for permission, and keep a bit of money aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be calmer than with 2028 but not at ease. By 2031 the thinking work shifts, and by 2034 the robots reach the shop floor, and I'm 32. That's time to change course without panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the technician pathway in year one, part-time, and aim to move into automation support within three years. I'd keep adding to savings with a target of three months, and I'd take a small stake in a robotics-related index fund. I'd also use AI to speed up my studying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but upbeat. A five-year window is like a long race, where you can pace yourself. I'd still check the numbers weekly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, what do you do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hannah, first. She's training to be a teacher, and teachers are a hands-on, people-based job, so that's good for us both. We'd talk about where to live, and what a future salary would need to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you take with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My team. Two of them would listen, and I'd bring them with me. The others would call me an alarmist, and I'd let it go.

Don't wait for **permission**, and keep a bit of money aside.

fieldNote: The longer window supports a **phased** plan: study, move, save.
Counts on his partner's **people-based** job as a stabiliser.
Accepts that some coworkers will **dismiss** him.

steps.text: Start the part-time technician pathway in year one
Use AI to speed up studying for the technician course
Put a small amount into a robotics-related index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's use it. I'd tell friends to pick one skill each year and keep an eye on where the money goes. I'd say it with a laugh, because I'd be excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel good about it. By 2036 I'd have a trade, maybe a small business, and by 2039 the robots would need people like me. For once the change looks like it works in my favour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the technician course, get a job at an automation firm within three or four years, and save for a deposit. I'd also keep the side project going and turn it into a small paid tool. I'd keep up with AI because it moves every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. I'd still have the money worry for a while, but I'd feel I was on a path. It's the first scenario where I feel like it's a fair deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you build?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I get distracted. I have a lot of side projects and I don't finish them all. Hannah is good at telling me to pick one, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with a long runway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably that the technician jobs also get automated by 2039. But I'd be aware of it, and I'd shift. Being adaptive is a habit, not a one-time thing.

say: Ten years is a **gift**, so use it, and pick one skill each year.
think: By 2036 I'd have a **trade**, and by 2039 the robots would need people like me.
For once the change looks like it works in my **favour**.
do: Finish the **technician** course and join an automation firm within three or four years.
Turn the side project into a small **paid tool**.
feel: **Calm**, because I'm on a path and it feels like a fair deal.
S4.quote: Being adaptive is a habit, not a one-time thing.
fieldNote: The long runway makes change look **favourable**, the only scenario that lifts him to calm.
His risk is **distraction**, and Hannah keeps him focused.
He expects even technician jobs to **change**, and plans to adapt again.

steps.text: Finish the technician course and join an automation firm

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Even with a plan, I've no savings, and two years is tight. What would help is a living grant while I retrain, employer-paid courses and rules that make firms tell staff early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe just that cashiers and pickers are the people who see where the technology breaks first. If you want to know whether the robot works, ask the person who has to clean up after it.

headlineQuote: If you want to know whether the robot works, ask the person who has to clean up after it.
portrait: Gareth is 27, a **team lead** on picking and tills at a supermarket with a big online business, paid below average.
He lives with Hannah (his partner), a trainee teacher, and has under a month saved, with few similar jobs nearby.
He uses AI every day, tinkers with a **side project**, and treats change as something to run towards.
His centre view shows in a **bargaining** stance: he wants a share of the savings he creates.
Across the scenarios he plans a **technician** career behind the robots, anxious in 2028 and calm only with ten years.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, since even a good plan can't beat having no savings.
whatWouldHelp: A **living grant** while retraining, employer-paid courses and early warning from firms.
